_comment: Memory-tier constants measured on the target machine. Every value here was produced by tools/bench_hardware.py and tools/bench_inference.py, not copied from a datasheet. Regenerate with `make doctor` / `make bench-inference`.

effective_capacity._comment: What a runtime actually obtains, measured rather than assumed. VRAM: the card has 8188 MiB but the desktop holds ~2.9 GiB and ollama peaked at 3906 MiB of model memory (6884 - 2978 MiB baseline). RAM: MemAvailable during the runs was 10.23e9 bytes = 9.5 GiB -- therefore GB, NOT GiB. Mixing the two units overstates the RAM tier by ~7%, which is why the key is named ram_usable_gb.
effective_capacity.note: Set vram_usable_gib to 0 to model a headless/display-free run.

calibration._comment: Decode rates measured end-to-end with ollama on this machine, used to check predicted_decode_tok_s.

known_limitations: NVMe throughput measures 0.8-1.9 GB/s against a ~6.6 GB/s datasheet figure for the Micron 3400. Cause not established (thermals, ASPM/APST power state, PCIe link width, or sustained-state fallback). A healthy drive would materially change the streaming budget; worth checking before designing around this number.

The RAM tier bandwidth is a memcpy figure (40.7 GB/s). Real quantised CPU GEMV kernels differ: a naive torch bf16 GEMV reached only 19.3 GB/s here, while llama.cpp int4 kernels evidently exceed 40 GB/s (ornith-1.5:9b ran at 24.6 tok/s with ~2.7 GB on CPU).

Tier capacities are effective, not physical: the tier model ignores that real runtimes overlap CPU and GPU work, so it over-predicts some configurations by up to ~1.7x. It is a ceiling estimator validated within ~2x on three measured points, not a forecast.
Vulkan/ROCm were not tested; only CUDA.
